title: Mismatch
intro: Two transistors drawn identically differ in threshold, mobility, oxide and dimensions by small random amounts. This sets the offset of every differential circuit, limits the accuracy of current copies, and lets even-order distortion and common-mode signals leak through (Razavi, Section 14.2).

blocks.text: Why bigger devices match better

Edges of the gate are rough on a microscopic scale, and dopant counts under the gate fluctuate. A wide device behaves like $n$ narrow ones in parallel, each with an independent length error $\Delta L_0$; their average has error $\Delta L_0/\sqrt{n}$. The same averaging applies to $V_{TH}$ and $\mu C_{ox}$ when a large device is viewed as many small ones in series and parallel, so all mismatches fall with area. Measured data follow

blocks.caption: Standard deviations; $A_{VTH}$ and $A_K$ come from measurement (Pelgrom's law).

blocks.text: Halving the mismatch costs four times the area, and with it four times the gate capacitance: matching trades directly against speed. Capacitor ratios match to about 0.1%, a measured rather than fundamental figure. Systematic errors from gradients and asymmetric layout are separate and are handled by layout (common centroid, same orientation, dummies).
Offset of a differential pair

blocks.alt: Schematic. A resistively loaded differential pair M1, M2 with tail source ISS (arrow down). Both gates are effectively grounded, but a voltage source VOS sits in series with the gate of M1. The output, between the drains, reads zero.
blocks.caption: The input-referred offset is the voltage that, placed in series with one input, returns the output to zero.

blocks.text: With $V_{in} = 0$, mismatches make $V_{out} \ne 0$. It is more useful to refer this to the input: $|V_{OS,in}| = |V_{OS,out}|/A_v$, the input that nulls the output. It limits, for example, the smallest difference a comparator can resolve, and in a chain of DC-coupled gain stages it can saturate the later ones. Let the loads differ by $\Delta R_D$, the sizes by $\Delta(W/L)$ and the thresholds by $\Delta V_{TH}$. Requiring $I_{D1}R_1 = I_{D2}R_2$ and expanding to first order:

Threshold mismatch goes straight to the input; size and load mismatch are scaled by half the overdrive, so a low overdrive (low current or wide devices) helps. The terms are independent random variables and add in power:
Offset of the five-transistor OTA

Model each pair's mismatch as a source in series with one gate. The NMOS input pair contributes its own term directly. The PMOS mirror's offset produces a current error $g_{mP}V_{OS,P}$ that the input pair must cancel, so it is divided by $g_{mN}$ when referred to the input, exactly as with noise:
Current-source mismatch
Two current sources sharing a gate voltage: take the total differential of $I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_{TH})^2$:

Here a large overdrive helps, the opposite of the input-pair rule, because a given threshold error is a smaller fraction of a large overdrive. Noise shows the same split: a pair's input noise voltage rises with overdrive at fixed current, a current source's output noise current rises with $g_m$.
Even-order distortion and thermal asymmetry

Odd symmetry kills even harmonics only if the halves match. With paths $y_1 = \alpha_1x + \alpha_2x^2 + \alpha_3x^3$ and $y_2 = \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2 + \beta_3x^3$ driven by $\pm x$, the differential output keeps $(\alpha_2 - \beta_2)x^2$, giving a second harmonic of amplitude $(\alpha_2 - \beta_2)A^2/2$. Phase mismatch at high frequency does the same, and a power-hungry block next to one device of a pair creates a temperature difference that shifts its $V_{TH}$ and mobility.

This makes some choices obvious. A PMOS input pair in its own n-well with source tied to bulk has thresholds independent of the input CM; with the bulk at $V_{DD}$, body effect makes the thresholds move with the CM, and any mismatch in body-effect coefficients turns into a CM-dependent offset, i.e. worse CMRR.

blocks.title: Pelgrom's law
blocks.text: $A_{VTH} = 5$ mV·µm. Find $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH})$ for $WL = 1\,\mu\text{m}^2$ and $25\,\mu\text{m}^2$.

blocks.title: Sizing for offset
blocks.text: In a process with $A_{VTH} = 3.5$ mV·µm, an input pair uses $L = 0.1\,\mu$m. What width keeps $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH}) \le 1$ mV?

blocks.title: Differential-pair offset
blocks.text: A resistively loaded pair has $V_{GS} - V_{TH} = 0.2$ V, $\sigma(\Delta R/R) = 1\%$, $\sigma(\Delta(W/L)/(W/L)) = 1\%$ and $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH}) = 2$ mV. Find $\sigma(V_{OS,in})$.

blocks.title: OTA offset
blocks.text: In a five-transistor OTA the NMOS pair contributes $V_{OS,N} = 1.5$ mV and the PMOS mirror $V_{OS,P} = 2$ mV, with $g_{mP}/g_{mN} = 0.5$. Find the input-referred offset.

blocks.title: Current mirror
blocks.text: Mirror devices have $V_{GS} - V_{TH} = 0.2$ V, $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH}) = 2$ mV and $\sigma(\Delta(W/L)/(W/L)) = 0.5\%$. Find $\sigma(\Delta I/I)$. What overdrive would halve the threshold part?
solution: Doubling the overdrive to 0.4 V halves the threshold part to 1%.

blocks.title: CMRR from offset drift
blocks.text: An amplifier's input-referred offset changes by 0.5 mV when its input common mode moves by 1 V. What is its CMRR?
